## Part 55: Chrome without friction, and fast browser and computer use (2026-10-17)

The owner's word of 2026-10-17: "Ajan kendi tarayıcısında sıfırdan başlamasın. Alabildiği her şeyi alsın; ben sorunsuz
Chrome üzerinde hızlı computer use ve browser use istiyorum." (the agent should not start from nothing in a browser of
its own but take all it can; smooth, fast computer use and browser use in Chrome.) Decided with it: the agent works in
the owner's live Chrome (`[browser] mode = "attach"`, My Chrome), as it is, copying nothing of what Chrome keeps on
disk; Chrome's remote-debugging switch and its Allow button stay the owner's, and the card and the errors say how. Done
when: the setup takes one Allow at most and a run finds the owner signed in; later runs connect with no click, and after
a restart of Chrome the next call connects again by itself with one clear line, never crashes and says why on a timeout;
Dot's tabs open in a window of their own, the app in front stays in front and the owner's tabs are not touched; (a)
browser_open to its first view, (b) a browser_act of three actions, (c) a computer-use loop and (d) a ten-step task are
measured before and after on the same Mac, none slower, the three slowest better or shown to be the model's or the
network's time; and the checks pass. Tests never touch the owner's Chrome (a scratch Chrome through `DOT_CHROME_DIR`);
the last real try is the owner's. Built on `items-339-chrome`; merged as #331 (`1bf81a1`).

**Measured** (ms; `tests/smoke/test_chrome_speed.py` against a hidden scratch Chrome in attach mode: five runs each
side, alternating with `main`, each the median of five calls, shown as the median of the five runs and their range;
`tests/smoke/test_desktop_speed.py` against the fixture window: the median of ten loops):

| Step                                                  | before (`main`)            | after                      |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| connect to Chrome (the driver started)                | 154.2 (152.4-154.9)        | 153.8 (152.5-154.5)        |
| (a) browser_open in a new chat (its tab is made)      | 125.5 (123.8-129.8)        | 211.1 (208.1-214.0)        |
| (a) browser_open again, in the chat's tab             | 103.1 (101.8-104.0)        | 100.7 (97.0-102.2)         |
| (b) browser_act of three actions                      | 229.5 (228.2-242.7)        | 166.5 (164.6-169.5)        |
| snapshot                                              | 75.7 (75.1-76.7)           | 72.7 (70.6-73.0)           |
| screenshot of the page                                | 23.6 (23.6-26.0)           | 20.6 (10.9-27.1)           |
| a page an app draws in frames, open and its text      | 187.8 (186.2-189.5)        | 177.4 (176.3-183.8)        |
| (c) screen, click, screen                             | 516.1, 518.6 (two runs)    | 479.4                      |
| (d) a ten-step task through the loop, scripted model  | 61,275.9                   | 1,470.2                    |

With the scratch Chrome on screen (`DOT_SPEED_VISIBLE=1`, three runs each side) the picture is the same: a new chat
121.5 against 195.2, the act of three 233.7 against 169.3, the snapshot 77.5 against 72.2, the app's page 180.8 against
174.6 (drawn five times in five on both sides), the page's screenshot 44.3 against 46.0 (ranges 34.8-46.7 and 45.5-48.0,
the same 1280 by 713 viewport). The one slower step is the first browser_open of a chat, which makes its tab in a window
of its own (item 340), with no gain in speed (see 340): the window takes about 30 ms more to make than a tab in the
owner's (44.5 against 14.1 ms with Chrome on screen; 56-73 against 17-19 ms hidden, where the harness also meets the new
window's renderer cold), paid once a chat, as its tabs stay until `tab_idle_s`, and for each quiet read (`read_page`,
the web tools' way through a page that needs JavaScript) and browser_new_tab. In the owner's runs of the last 30 days
(`dotx stats`) a step's model call takes 5 to 7 s and the median browser_open 1.2 s, most of it the network; the three
slowest of Dot's own steps above are the ten-step task, the computer-use loop and the three-action act, all faster.

### 339. Back in the owner's Chrome takes a navigation, not 30 s

**Status: done (`1bf81a1`).** **As built (2026-10-17).** A Chrome that keeps its back-forward cache (the owner's;
Playwright's own Chrome turns it off) brings the page Back from the cache with no DOMContentLoaded and no load event:
`go_back(wait_until="domcontentloaded")` waited the whole navigation timeout, 30 s, and then failed though the tab had
gone back, and the settle after a click that went back waited the same in `_wait_quiet`. `go_back` now waits for the
commit and first asks Chrome's history whether a page is before (Dot's blank start does not count), and `_wait_quiet`
reads `document.readyState` in the page. Measured: browser_back in the ten-step task 30,000 ms before, 110 after. Test:
`test_browser_attach.py::test_back_in_the_chrome_of_the_user_takes_no_longer_than_a_page` (fails on `main`).

### 340. A tab of Dot's in the owner's Chrome opens in a window of its own

**Status: done (`1bf81a1`).** **As built (2026-10-17).** In attach mode `_background_tab` makes the tab with
`Target.createTarget` and `newWindow` besides `background`: the window opens behind the window the owner works in, the
app in front stays in front (measured: Finder before and after), and the owner's windows and tabs are not touched. With
Chrome itself in front, as when the owner works in it, the window opens below the owner's and Chrome stays the app in
front (measured after the review with the window order Quartz gives). Measured first in a scratch Chrome on screen (one
second of frames and timer ticks): a tab made in the background of the owner's window is hidden, 0 frames and 8 ticks; a
window of its own 61 and 208, also when another window covers it whole; a minimized one is hidden again, so Dot never
minimizes. After the review, an A/B with the scratch Chrome on screen drew an app's page in both, which a probe
explained: `keep_focused`, the focus emulation Dot puts on every tab of its in the owner's Chrome, has a tab made in the
background draw at 61 frames and 208 ticks too. So the window buys no speed: it keeps Dot's tabs out of the owner's
windows, which criterion 3 asks, at the cost in the table above. One window per tab; the window goes with its tab. Test:
`test_browser_attach.py::test_a_tab_of_dot_opens_in_a_window_of_its_own` (Chrome's own `Browser.getWindowForTarget`).

### 341. A restarted Chrome is said in one line, and the card follows Chrome

**Status: done (`1bf81a1`).** **As built (2026-10-17).** The connection stays across runs (only a switch, closing the session
or a new DevTools port of Dot's own Chrome drops it), so later runs need no click. When Chrome quits or restarts the
session marks itself lost; the next call connects again by itself, the owner gets a notification ("Chrome asks to allow
Dot"), the connection's error starts with "Chrome was closed or restarted", and a step under way when Chrome went fails
with that line and that the next step connects again. Settings › Browser reads the session's `lost` and `waiting_allow`
every 3 s while the card is open in attach mode: connected, waiting for Allow, Chrome closed, remote debugging off,
Chrome restarted or not connected, each with one line of what to do. After the review the notice is told beside the
connection, never in its way: one that fails (osascript, a notification macOS did not show) was the error of every later
call, as the session stayed lost; and a connection whose wait ran out says so ("no answer within 60 s"). Tests in
`test_browser_attach.py`: `test_a_session_reports_that_chrome_has_quit_and_works_again_when_chrome_is_back`,
`test_a_chrome_that_restarted_and_refuses_says_so_in_one_line`,
`test_a_reconnection_whose_notice_fails_connects_all_the_same` (fails on `main`'s 341) and
`test_the_settings_card_follows_chrome_as_it_quits_and_comes_back`.

### 342. A browser step waits for what it set off, not for a fixed 40 ms

**Status: done (`1bf81a1`).** **As built (2026-10-17).** After a step that can open a tab or a dialog, `_let_events_land`
slept `side_effect_grace_ms` (40 ms) and then waited for the popups Playwright had reported. Probes showed that one turn
of the page's event loop is enough for Chrome to have told of a dialog, a file chooser, a navigation in the document and
a tab it made, thirty times in thirty in both modes, and that Playwright reports a new tab only once its page has
answered: 411 ms after the click for a page that answers in 400 ms, while Chrome tells of it about 8 ms before the click
returns. So the grace let a batch go on past a popup whose page answers late. Now the page takes one turn
(`let_page_turn`, a `setTimeout(0)` in the page; Playwright holds it while a navigation the step started is under way,
until it commits), and each tab keeps the tabs Chrome made for it (`watch_births`: a CDP session of the tab's own with
`Target.setDiscoverTargets`; births whose opener is the tab, gone when the thread takes them in or Chrome closes them).
The step waits until each is taken in, a second at most; one still opening then stops the batch with "a new tab is
opening and its page has not answered yet". A popup Chrome blocks (the second of one click, in the owner's Chrome) is no
birth and holds nothing, where `Page.windowOpen` would have counted it. After the review a popup that could not be
registered no longer holds its opener's next step (`_adopt_popup` lets go of its birth on every way out), and the CDP
session's errors are `BrowserError`s as `keep_focused`'s are. The window's size is read alongside the snapshot instead
of before it: no round trip of its own, and never stale, where a size kept until the window is resized would need a
listener in the page or a poll of Chrome to tell that the owner resized Dot's window. `[browser] side_effect_grace_ms`
is gone. Tests: `test_browser.py::test_a_tab_whose_page_answers_late_still_stops_the_batch` and
`::test_a_tab_still_opening_when_the_wait_ends_stops_the_batch_and_joins_later` (both fail on `main`: the batch went
on), `test_browser_attach.py::test_a_click_that_asks_for_two_tabs_stops_at_the_one_chrome_opened`.

### 343. Computer use checks only what it needs, and "Google Chrome" is the Chrome Dot works in

**Status: done (`1bf81a1`).** **As built (2026-10-17).** Measured on the act's path: each preparation read all three
permissions, 13 ms, where Screen Recording and input events take 6.4 ms each and Accessibility nothing; listing the
applications (`lsappinfo`) takes 25 ms and ran for the preview and again for the act. Now an act reads Accessibility and
input events, a screenshot Screen Recording only, and the act uses the preview's listing when it follows within a second

control that names remote debugging or chrome://inspect's page), since the errors of item 341 tell the owner to click

`desktop_screenshot` with a region zooms) and its LANCZOS resize (a box reduce first saves 17 ms a screenshot but moves

`test_browser_attach.py::test_a_script_reaches_the_runs_own_tab_every_time_while_three_chromes_run`, the desktop smoke
tests, and `tests/smoke/test_desktop_speed.py` for the loop's numbers.

free call). What a model can do comes from OpenRouter's own list of its models (`GET /models`, read again after

it takes a temperature, its reasoning levels (`reasoning.supported_efforts`; read on 2026-10-17: 470 models, 399 with

back on the same model's next step beside its tool calls (`ChatOptions.replay_details`), as OpenRouter asks; the chat

page not shaped as OpenRouter documents it is a `ProviderProtocolError`, and `dotx doctor` checks a configured model
against the list before asking about it, so a list that could not be read is the warning beside the provider's row. No

### 359. A phone takes Dot's new pages over a slow network too

**Status: done (`83d81e3`).** The owner's word of 2026-10-18: "mobilde yeni composer'ı hâlâ göremiyorum" (on the phone I
still do not see the new composer, item 352). **As built (2026-10-18).** The phone's service worker answers a page from
its kept copy when the network has not answered within 200 ms (item 328), and dropped the network's answer that came
later: the copy was renewed only by an answer within 200 ms. A phone that reaches the Mac through Tailscale, slower than
that on every request, kept opening the build it first kept, and the one reload a page of another build makes was
answered from the same copy. `sw.js` now notes a late answer that names another build than the copy's, as the name of an
empty cache, which outlives the service worker iOS stops between openings; the next opening waits for the network up to
5 seconds, so that the page and its files come from that build and are kept whole. The copy answers until then, when the
network fails, and when it has not answered within those 5 seconds, as when the Mac is out of reach and its connections
hang rather than fail; it stays whole for that. Tests: `tests/smoke/test_phone_return.py`, after an update on a network
always slower than the wait (the test proxy's `slow`): the copy answers and stays whole, the newer build is noted, an
opening while the Mac is out of reach (the proxy's `sleep`) is answered by the copy once the 5 seconds are over and
keeps the note, and the next opening keeps the newer build whole, which fails on the code before. The waits on a page's
caches are made real: Playwright's `wait_for_function` takes the promise of an async function for true at once, so the
two helpers that waited for the service worker's copy (`test_phone_return.py`, `test_reconnect.py`) waited for nothing.
Docs: `docs/phone.md`.

### 389. The harness: what Dot improves around its model, and its first layer, the versions a run's prompt takes

**Status: done (2026-10-19), on `harness-1`, stacked on `js-gate`.** The owner's word of 2026-10-19 ("Prompts → Agents →
Loops → Graphs → Harness; ön araştırma, ardından profesyonel şekilde"): Dot's model is fixed, the soft parts around it
are what makes a given model work well here, and nothing improved them with evidence. **Research.** Harness² (Xu et al.,
arXiv 2610.14224; google-research/harness2, Apache-2.0): eight editable components mounted as files, a
Propose–Probe–Compose step per task (two candidates, one about how the agent works and one about what a practitioner
knows; probes beside a reference; a composer that keeps, revises or drops each edit on an observed moment, or keeps the
base), parallel or sequential recursion with budget k, an experience library with cue/lesson/evidence/confidence entries
written only when execution contrasts support them, and a blind selector. Taken as the method, not the code: it is a
Linux research harness over OpenCode/Codex with Vertex model ids, three commits and no release. A survey of Dot's own
layers (prompt assembly, lessons/reflection/playbooks, evals, agents, API/UI patterns) is in `docs/harness.md`'s shape
and in this item's decisions. **As built (this layer, Prompts).** `docs/harness.md` says what the harness holds and what
never changes without the owner. A version of the harness (`harness_versions`, a record `HarnessVersion`) holds two
texts, *habits* (after how to work) and *tool guidance* (after the tools and the rules of communication), who made it,
what it was made from, its state (candidate, probed, adopted, retired), a summary and its notes; `[harness]` bounds each
text (1,200 and 1,500 characters, 16 lines, no line past 300), and a text with a secret, a link, an e-mail address, a
home path or an account name is refused, as a lesson's is, and so is one with a character that does not print. Every
run's system prompt takes the adopted version's texts (`agent/prompt.py`, both styles, under leads that name the trust
rules as the ones that win), and records the version it took (`runs.harness_version`). `dotx harness
list|show|diff|set|adopt|retire` and `GET/POST /api/harness…` write, adopt (which retires the one adopted before;
adopting an earlier one again takes a change back) and retire versions; the daemon reads the adopted one as each run
starts, no restart. **Decisions.** Addenda, not rewrites: the loop (and the owner) add bounded sections under Dot's own
text rather than editing the 14k-character prompt, so a weaker review model can propose safely and the trust, safety and
secrets lines stay as tests pin them. Domain knowledge keeps going to learned skills (playbooks), which have their own
validation; the harness holds the invariant scope. Roles of the loop are config, not agent records (an agent with no
tool list gets every tool and learns for itself). The store keeps versions and the adopted pointer (`kv
harness.adopted`); files on disk would duplicate state. **Next layers.** Agents (the proposer, composer, selector and
reflector as typed roles on `[models] review`), Loops (the probe in a throwaway home on the eval tasks safe to repeat,
the nightly step after the reflection with budgets and a health record), Graphs (provenance: version ← probe ← run,
experience → version, the decisions of each step), Harness (the owner's page).

### 390. The harness: the roles of the improvement loop

**Status: done (2026-10-19), on `harness-2`, stacked on `harness-1`.** The second layer (Agents): the four roles of the
step as typed questions to a model, answered with one tool call each, in `agent/review.py` beside Dot's other questions:
the proposer (`propose_harness`: the whole texts of a candidate within the bounds, the moments of the run behind each
change, or keep; a scope of how the agent works or of what a practitioner knows), the composer (`compose_harness`: one
version of the candidates and what their probes showed, a decision with its evidence for each change, or the base kept),
the blind selector (`select_answer`: the best of anonymous answers, judged on delivery, conformance, fidelity,
consistency, fitness and finish, never length) and the experience writer (`write_experience`: what each edit did,
helped/hurt/no_effect/confounded, and an experience of cue, lesson, evidence and confidence only when an edit helped or
hurt). Each answer is checked (`proposal_check`, `composition_check`, `selection_check`, `experience_check`): a text
past the bounds or with a secret, a link or an address, a change with no moment, keep with a text that differs from the
one in place, a decision naming no candidate, an experience with no effect behind it or whose lines could not stand in a
prompt (a link, a secret, an address), is asked again with what was wrong, as the review model's other answers are. What
a run read stands inside fences the roles are told to read and never follow; the secrets Dot holds are masked as in
every review question. `[harness] proposer|composer|selector|experience` name a model each, "" for `[models] review`;
the call purposes `harness_propose|compose|select|experience` count in `dotx stats`. `dotx harness propose RUN_ID
[--scope]` asks the proposer about one run by hand (the run as the reflection reads it: digest, failed calls, stalls,
send-backs, whether it read outside content) and writes its candidate, made by `proposer`, with the scope, the moments
and the taint in its notes. **Research taken in.** Wei et al., "The End of Harness Engineering" (2026): the human's
artifact is the scoring set, never shown to the proposer; a final set is run once and never optimized against; the best
edit by score survives. docs/harness.md says so, and the probe (next item) keeps a final set apart. From the Grok Bot
build notes: charters of owns / done looks like / stops at, and "a figure without its source and read time goes back to
the desk it came from", kept as the first example habits and as a candidate check for the page's "keep this run as a
test".

### 391. The harness: the probe and the nightly step

**Status: done (2026-10-19), on `harness-3`, stacked on `harness-2`.** The third layer (Loops). A probe
(`harness/probe.py`) plays one text on the scoring set: each task a run in a throw-away home with the exclusions of an
eval, the text adopted in the attempt's own store before its run starts (`play(..., harness)` in the eval runner), a
scorecard per attempt (passed, ending, cut, steps, tokens, tool errors, seconds), and a stop before the attempt that
would pass the budget of minutes or tokens, the next attempt taken to cost what the earlier ones did; a process that
outlives its budget is ended and counts as cut short, and ended too when the daemon stops (SIGTERM, which the probe
answers by cancelling its play so that the commands it started end with it; SIGKILL after a grace). A probe runs in a
process of its own (`dotx harness probe --ask FILE`, JSON in and out): an attempt switches the process's Dot home, which
the daemon must never see. The contrast (`harness/contrast.py`) says per task whether a candidate passed more, as often
or less than the base, and in all better (more on a task, less on none), same, worse or unclear (a probe cut short); the
candidate better on the most tasks, then the cheapest, survives. The step (`harness/step.py`) learns from the newest run
of the owner's that ended since the last step, proposes in each scope, probes the base and the candidates within the
budget, keeps the survivor as `probed` (two that both did better are merged by the composer and the merge is played in
its turn; it survives when it did better, else the best candidate does), retires the rest with their contrasts, writes
what each edit did and an experience when one helped or hurt (`harness_experiences`), records itself (`harness_steps`,
`harness_probes`), and adopts on its own only with `[harness] adopt = "auto"` and two repeats, never from a run that had
read content third parties can author; a composer or experience writer that fails leaves the step failed with the error,
the survivor probed all the same, and a scripted check does not move the next step's window. The scheduler runs it at
`[harness] step_time` ("off" by default: every run of a probe spends the main model's tokens; the eight small tasks
twice under three texts are about fifty runs), timed and recorded like the reflection, under learning health's new work
`harness`; `dotx harness step` runs it by hand and `--scripted` plays the references through the scripted model, the
whole loop at no cost, which the smoke test does. `dotx harness final` plays the final set once under the adopted
version and keeps the report in the version's notes. **Decisions.** Score first, composer second: the best by the
scoring set survives; the composer merges only two winners. Probes apart from the daemon, not in it: `eval_environment`
is process-wide. The default is off until the owner chooses a budget; the page (item 393) will carry the switch. **Left
for later.** A scoring set with headroom: the first step with a real model (Claude Haiku 5.5) passed the eight tasks 2/2
under the base and the candidate alike, so the loop can only keep until the set holds tasks the main model fails
sometimes; and a secondary signal (steps, tokens) when pass rates tie.

### 392. The harness: provenance

**Status: done (2026-10-19), on `harness-4`, stacked on `harness-3`.** The fourth layer (Graphs). `harness/graph.py`
reads the store into a graph: versions (made from, composed of), steps (learned from a run, proposed candidates, probed
the survivor), experiences (about a version, written in a step) and the runs learned from, and draws it as a Mermaid
flowchart; a version's lineage is its ancestors, the attempts of its probes, the steps that touched it (as base,
candidate or probed version) and the experiences about it. `GET /api/harness/graph|steps|experiences` and `GET
/api/harness/{id}/lineage`; `dotx harness graph|steps|experiences`, and `show` ends with the lineage. The library is
read: the proposer is shown the newest experiences before it writes; an experience written from a run that had read
content third parties can author is kept marked `tainted` and never shown to it (the rule of item 384's notes).
**Decision.** The graph is read from the tables the step already writes (`harness_versions.parent_id`, the notes'
`composed_of`, the steps' outcome, the probes and experiences by version), not from an edge table of its own: one source
of truth, nothing to keep in step.

**Status: done (2026-10-19), on `item-398-approval-modes`, for the owner to merge (it changes `src/dotagent/policy/`).**
The owner's word of 2026-10-19: "Mevcut sistemimizdeki Auto ve Ask modlarinin mantigini düzeltelim meseal auto modda bir

before commands and file changes), Auto-accept edits (auto-approve edits, ask before other actions), Auto (supported

### 399. A path is classified by the place it names, through the Data volume too

**Status: done (2026-10-19), on `item-399-kernel-paths`, for the owner to merge (it changes `src/dotagent/policy/`).**
Found by the `/security-review` of item 398, as a finding older than that item: macOS joins its Data volume to the
system volume with firmlinks, so `/System/Volumes/Data/Users/<owner>/.ssh/id_rsa` is `~/.ssh/id_rsa` and
`/System/Volumes/Data/private/tmp/…` is `/tmp/…`, and `realpath` follows links, not firmlinks; spelled so, a path
escaped its class: a protected file read as a `system` one, with neither the refusal of a secret nor a question, and a
file of Dot's own was no `dot` path. **As built.** `policy/paths.kernel_path` names a path as the kernel does: the
deepest folder on it that the daemon can open is opened for its events alone (`O_EVTONLY`, which reads nothing of it,
with `O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW`, so that a file, a pipe, a device or a link is never opened: a pipe nobody writes to
would hold the open, and opening a device can wake it) and asked its path (`F_GETPATH`); the rest of the path follows.
`expand_path` (every path a tool, the shell guard or OpenCode's permissions name), `expand_protected` (the protected
locations and Dot's own paths) and the workspace in `classify_path` go through it, so both sides of a comparison name
places the same way; letter case was already set aside (`within`, item 116). Tests: `tests/unit/test_kernel_paths.py` (a
protected file through the Data volume is protected and its read refused, a new file in Dot's own folder is `dot`, a
missing place keeps its name after the folder the kernel names, a pipe nobody writes to is named at once, a folder
closed to reading through the folder it is in). Docs: `docs/safety.md`. The `/security-review` of this item found three
spellings more, older than it, fixed here as the same class: a file named by its number (`/.vol/<device>/<inode>`, which
no folder can name: a path, a glob or a text in that namespace, behind `/.nofollow` too, now reaches every protected
location), a link the command line made (the shell guard resolved the path behind it with `realpath` alone; now with
`kernel_path`), and a glob that spells the Data volume (`/S*/V*/D*/U*/…`; a glob is now matched against every spelling
of a location: as it is, through the Data volume, behind `/.nofollow`, and both); with them, one this item brought:
`mentions_protected` compared a `$HOME` in other letters with the kernel-named locations letter by letter (now letter
case aside). Each has a test that fails without its fix. The pre-push review of those fixes (0 Important) named two more
of the class, fixed too: the prefix `/.resolve/<flags>`, which names the root again as `/.nofollow` does, and the links
at the root (`/var`, `/tmp`, `/etc` into `/private`), which a glob or a text could spell a protected location through; a
glob is now matched through every other name of the root (`_glob_reaches`), a text through the links too, and the home
folder's spellings are made part by part, so a letter whose case folding changes its length cannot cut them wrong.

### 404. The first answer's delay: a prompt the provider's cache keeps, and the skills' embeddings ready

**Status: done (2026-10-19), on `item-404-first-token`.** The owner's word of 2026-10-19: "providerların ilk response
başlama olayı neden 30+ saniye sürüyor? Bu gecikmenin arkasında yatan problem nedir? Bunu araştırmanı ve tüm providerlar
için düzeltmeni talep ediyorum" (why does the first response of the providers take 30+ seconds, what is behind it, find
it and fix it for every provider). **Measured** on the owner's chat runs of the day (`opencode_go:deepseek-v4.1-flash`):
every message is a new run, and its first model call carried 185,000 to 221,000 input tokens of which 3,200 came from
the provider's cache, against the whole prompt for the later steps of the same run; so the first step took 20 to 48
seconds and the later ones 2 to 15. The cause: the instructions changed from message to message, with the skills listed
by the message's words and the notes recalled for it, in front of the whole history, so the cached prefix ended after
3,200 tokens. Three runs waited another 31 to 88 seconds between their `memories` and `scaffold` events: the first run
after each start of the daemon embedded the texts of 433 skills through Ollama's `bge-m3` in one call of about 148,000
characters, which took half a minute when it worked and broke Ollama's model runner (`/tokenize: EOF`, 25 times in the
log) when it did not. **As built (2026-10-19).** The instructions list the skills that fit the chat's first words (its
title), the same at every message, and hold no recalled notes; what changes with the message goes under it, in the
stored note that gave the time (`turn_note`): the notes recalled for it that no earlier message of the chat carries, how
many were left out as tainted, and up to six more skills that fit it. Stored, the note is the same bytes at the next
message, so the provider's cache holds up to the message after it. The skills' embeddings are made 32 texts a call, kept
in the store across restarts (`help_vectors`), and made as the daemon starts in the background; a run that finds more
than 64 of them missing ranks its skills by words that once, without a warning (`HelpVectorsCold`). The tools' order in
the instructions follows the chat's title too, and a compaction of the run that folds the note away has it handed again
after the summary (the review's findings); its second round: `find_help` ranks by words while the texts are embedded in
the background, as the run's start does; the texts the model reads say where the notes come now; one warming at a time;
and the vectors no search asked for in thirty days, or another model's, go at the warming (`used_at`); its fourth round:
a note handed earlier in the chat comes again when its text changed since, and one forgotten since is named under the
message, as the old text stays in the chat; its fifth to seventh: after a compaction, told by the ledger's count, every
note the context lost comes back and only that (`recalled_again`), a forgotten note is named once (`forgotten_unnamed`),
a warming takes the texts asked for while it runs, and a search holds its own vectors against a cut meanwhile; its
eighth: the note handed again bears the system note's head, as every stored note does, so the goal's review reads it as
data. Every `model_call` event says how long its first streamed word took (`first_token_seconds`), so the delay is
measured from now on. Left as it was: the fast model's summary failures in the log were an earlier fast model's quota,
and the owner's `[models] fast` is the main model since; the SSL `BAD_RECORD_MAC` retries on reused connections are
rare. Tests: `tests/unit/test_run_modes.py` (the note), `test_help.py` (batches, the cold start, the keeper),
`test_model_calls.py` (the first word's seconds). Docs: `docs/memory-and-schedules.md`, `docs/extending.md`,
`docs/development.md`.
### 405. SnapShots: a double tap of ⌘ captures the window in front into the open chat's box

**Status: done (2026-10-19), on `item-405-snapshots`.** The owner's word of 2026-10-19, with a picture of another coding
agent's Settings › SnapShots (SnapShots, Include app text, Capture shortcut ⌘ ⌘, Capture sound, Capture flash, Capture
animations): "bu sistemi bizim projeye de kur" (build this system in our project too). **As built (2026-10-19).**
`desktop/snapshots.py`: a listen-only event tap of the session on a thread of its own watches the Command key through a
`TapDetector` (two presses within `[snapshots] double_tap_ms`, the key released between them, no other key from the
first press on, so ⌘C ⌘V is not a tap; it reads no key's identity); a double tap captures the window in front
(`screen.windows_on_screen` and `apps.frontmost_pid`, ScreenCaptureKit's rectangle capture with the password managers
blacked out, kept as sharp as the display up to 2000 px) and, with `app_text`, the window's accessibility tree as the
model reads it (`ax.snapshot`, `render.fit_lines`, 12,000 characters) as a Markdown file; both are stored as attachments
(`store_attachment`) and kept by the `SnapshotService` until a composer claims them (`POST /api/snapshots/claim`), the
system sound of the choice plays (`NSSound`: Tink, Pop, Glass), and a live `snapshot_taken` event tells the pages; a
capture that fails (`snapshot_failed`: Dot's own window, a password manager, no window, no permission) tells them why.
The box with a draft of its own (`composerFrame`, `js/snapshots.js`) takes the captures as they come and the ones that
waited, with a spring (`attach-chip.arrived`, none with reduced motion). Settings › SnapShots (`views/snapshots.js`, the
tab under This Mac) switches it live and in the config file (`config_edit` learned `[snapshots]`) and says whether the
key is watched or why not. The watch needs Accessibility granted to the app that runs Dot, which the desktop already
needs. The review's findings: the watch is tried again every few seconds while the permission is missing and the page's
reason clears by itself; a capture's files past the ten of a message are left out at the box with a notice; a capture
whose files cannot be stored tells the pages why, as one refused does. **Left for later:** the flash on the captured
window (the daemon has no AppKit run loop for a window of its own; the shell could draw it), a shortcut of the owner's
own, and the capture of one window alone (`SCContentFilter`) where the rectangle shows what lies over it. Tests:
`tests/unit/test_snapshots.py` (the tap, the names, the service), `tests/unit/test_config_edit.py`,
`tests/smoke/test_snapshots.py` (the routes with a capture in place of the window, the page, the box taking a capture),
`test_phone_settings.py` and `test_phone_pages.py` (the tab). Docs: `docs/daemon.md`.

### 417. A terminal session keeps what a program printed as it ended

**Status: done (2026-10-19), on `faz10-cleanup`.** The gate of the pull request of items 411 to 415 failed once on the
sandbox's terminal test: for a `cat` the sandbox refused, the session said "[no new output]" and "[the program ended
with exit 1]", without the refusal. **As built (2026-10-19).** Dot closed its copy of the terminal's other end as soon
as the program started, so the program's exit closed it last; macOS then keeps what the program printed last from the
read side, and a program that leads its session (each session's zsh does) waits in its exit for that output to drain,
for good (`ps` showed such programs `E`, trying to exit). With forty sessions at once, every output was lost. Dot now
holds that end until the program has exited, takes what it printed last, then closes it
(`TerminalSession.release_follower`); a session closed by hand takes nothing more. Tests: `tests/smoke/test_terminal.py`
(forty programs that print and end at once: each output is read and each session ends; without the change every output
is lost).

### 418. What would act for a run outside its sandbox is refused: open, launchd, Apple Events

**Status: done (2026-10-19), on `sandbox-escapes`; it changes `src/dotagent/policy/sandbox.py`, so the owner merges
it.** The owner's word of 2026-10-19: sandbox-exec did not cover the programs opened with `open`, launchd or Apple
Events; add those paths to the policy's filter. **As built (2026-10-19).** Outside yolo, the profile every process of a
run starts in (a shell command, a terminal session, an AppleScript, a search) also refuses what would have another
program act for it outside the sandbox: opening anything through Launch Services (`(deny lsopen)`: `open`, a program's
own call; measured: `open -a` fails with -54 and the application does not start), starting `launchctl`, `shortcuts` and
`lsregister` where macOS installs them (`HANDING_PROGRAMS`), creating a job of launchd (`(deny job-creation)`), and
writing into `~/Library/LaunchAgents`; like the guard's, these rules are best-effort. Apple Events were part of it and
are not: `(deny appleevent-send (appleevent-destination …))` over the terminal apps, Script Editor, Automator,
Shortcuts, System Events, the Finder and Xcode compiles and holds nothing (measured 2026-10-20, the note below says
what happened), so it was dropped rather than claimed. `desktop_open_app` given a bundle path that does not resolve onto
the sealed system volume (under `/System`, not the data volume at `/System/Volumes/Data`) asks first, as a step outside
the sandbox (`_bundle_of` with `_on_the_sealed_system_volume`): such a bundle may be one a run made, and `open` reads a
bare `x.app` from the daemon's folder. The shell and AppleScript tools say what the sandbox refuses and that
`desktop_open_app` opens an application. The owner's runs of this Mac measured the cost: of 542 shell lines none used
`open`, three used `osascript` (Calendar) and one `launchctl print`; 65 of 72 runs were yolo, where the sandbox does not
apply. Tests: `tests/unit/test_sandbox_profile.py` (the rules, and macOS holding a command to them: a job left in a
LaunchAgents folder, `launchctl`, `shortcuts`, `open -a`), `tests/smoke/test_sandbox.py` (the daemon's sandbox names the
user's LaunchAgents and refuses `launchctl` outside yolo only), `tests/unit/test_desktop_secrets.py`. Docs:
`docs/safety.md`, `docs/browser-and-computer-use.md`, `defaults.toml`.

**After the pre-push review (2026-10-20).** The review refused a copy of a handing program (`cp /usr/bin/shortcuts
/tmp/s`), which the path rules would not cover, and a bundle a run made that is opened by the name or bundle id it
registered. Measured on this Mac: a copy of an Apple program is killed by macOS itself before it runs (`cp /bin/echo
/tmp/e && /tmp/e` exits 137 with no output, in the sandbox and outside it, on Apple silicon under macOS 26), so that
route is closed; the service behind the program is refused instead, whatever program asks it (`HANDING_SERVICES`:
`com.apple.siri.VoiceShortcuts.xpc`, which runs a shortcut, and `com.apple.lsd.modifydb`, the Launch Services database).
Measured: with that rule `shortcuts list` fails ("Couldn't communicate with a helper application"), `lsregister -f`
prints "failed to scan … -10822" and registers nothing (0 dump entries against 3 when allowed), and a job of launchd
copy or not is refused. The tool's own review then found the check reading the path's letters as they came
(`/System/volumes/data` is the data volume too, on a file system that ignores case) and deciding on a resolution that
`open` made again later: the comparison is casefolded now, and the tool is a `make_path_tool`, classified again as it
starts and refused when the bundle it reaches is not the one authorised, as the file tools are (item 181). A later pass
kept the bundle apart from the words the call was given: the action carries the resolved bundle (`ActionInfo.bundle`)
and `run` opens that, while its target stays the application's name, which the runs at work at the same time (items 301
and 305) and the owner's rules read. The Apple
Events rule of the first commit was measured and found to hold nothing: on macOS 26
`(deny appleevent-send (appleevent-destination …))`, with or without a destination, still let a script drive the Finder
("26.4"), a terminal app, and start an application that was not running (Image Events), so the rule and its list are
gone and `docs/safety.md` says the gap is open; the Automation permission (TCC) and the policy's reading of the script
are what stand in its way. `desktop_open_app` now resolves a name or a bundle id through Launch Services
(`desktop.apps.bundle_path`) and judges the path it resolves to, so a run that registers a bundle it made in
`~/Applications` does not get it opened without a question (measured: ad-hoc signed and registered, the bundle id
resolves and `open -b` starts it); `names_a_bundle` is the one definition of a bundle path, `.app` in any letter case,
which is how the Mac's file systems and `open` read it; the sealed system volume is `/System` without the data volume
at `/System/Volumes/Data`, which puts Apple's own applications under `/System/Volumes/Preboot/Cryptexes` (Safari) on
the installed side. Tests: the service rule and both programs held to it (`tests/unit/test_sandbox_profile.py`), the
name and the bundle id (`tests/unit/test_desktop_secrets.py`).

### 422. The official sign-ins of Google and Microsoft, their tokens in the Keychain

**Status: done (2026-10-20), on `google-microsoft-sign-in`.** The owner's word of 2026-10-19: Gmail and Calendar through
OAuth rather than AppleScript and Chrome's cookies, official flows for Google and Microsoft, and the tokens in the
Keychain. **As built (2026-10-20).** `dotagent.oauth`: the providers (Google's Desktop app client with its secret,
Microsoft's public client), PKCE (S256) and a state good once, the code traded for tokens and the account named by its
address (Google's `email`, Microsoft's `mail` or user name), an access token refreshed once it is about to run out (the
refresh token kept when the provider gives no new one), signing out. The clients are read as Dot's keys are
(`DOT_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID`, `DOT_GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET`, `DOT_MS_CLIENT_ID`: environment, `.env`, the Keychain's
`dot-agent`); the tokens of each account are in the login Keychain under `dot-oauth`, written through `security`'s own
prompt so that no token is on a command line, in pieces short enough for a line of that prompt and in one of two slots
named last, so that tokens cut off half-written leave the ones before whole, and the list of accounts in the store. The browser comes back to the
daemon's `/oauth/callback`, which hands it to the accounts first and to an MCP server's sign-in otherwise; a sign-in
starts only from this Mac's own address. Customize › Plugins opens on an Accounts card with Sign in, the accounts and
Sign out. Nothing logs a token, a code or an address. The tools that use the accounts (Gmail, Google Calendar) are the
next item. Tests: `tests/unit/test_oauth.py`, `tests/smoke/test_oauth_accounts.py` (a stand-in provider that checks PKCE
and the client, a throw-away keychain), `tests/smoke/test_oauth_routes.py`; the smoke tests' `DOT_KEYCHAIN` names a
missing keychain, so that none touches the owner's. Docs: `docs/extending.md`, `docs/safety.md`.

### 432. The first release, 0.1.0: the signed and notarized Mac app, its disk image, and updates by itself

**Status: done (2026-10-20), on `release-0.1.0`; a path a human merges (`desktop/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json`, REVIEW.md),
merged on the owner's word of 2026-10-20 to merge every open branch once all was done; publishing is the owner's.** The
owner's word of 2026-10-19: "Sürüm hazırla. İmzalı bir Mac uygulaması, kurulum paketi ve otomatik güncelleme ekle.
CHANGELOG.md'yi de ilk sürüme göre güncelle." **As built.** The shell carries `tauri-plugin-updater`, used from Rust
only (no page gets its commands): it reads `latest.json` of the latest GitHub release as it starts and from the menu bar
item's new **Check for Updates…**, offers a newer version in a native dialog (rfd's, shown from Rust:
`tauri-plugin-dialog` would put its own `alert` and `confirm` in every page), and on **Install and Restart** downloads
it, checks its minisign signature against the public key in `tauri.conf.json`, which must also name the version offered
(`requireSignedVersion`, so that a tampered `latest.json` cannot pair a new number with an older signed archive),
installs it and starts again. One look at a time (`Looking`): the menu's during another says so. The look at start
speaks only when it finds an update; the one from the menu also says that Dot is the newest, or why it could not look.
`desktop/release.sh` builds a release on the owner's Mac from a clean checkout: the universal app signed with the one
Developer ID Application identity of the keychain (hardened runtime, secure timestamp), notarized with notarytool's
profile `dot-notary` and stapled; the updater's archive of the stapled app (no extended attributes), signed with
`~/.tauri/dot.key`, its password read from the Keychain (`dot-release`), bound to the version; the disk image (the app
and a link to Applications) signed, notarized and stapled; `latest.json` for both kinds of Mac; the changelog's section
as the notes. It checks first that the checkout is a commit of GitHub's `main` with nothing uncommitted, that the five
files of the version agree, that the tag is not on GitHub and that the public key is the key's, and it publishes
nothing: it prints the `gh release create` command, whose tag also publishes the package on PyPI.
`tests/unit/test_version.py` keeps the desktop app's version the package's; `~/.tauri` joins `[policy] protected_paths`.
The docs no longer say there is no check for updates. Docs: `docs/development.md` (Releasing), `docs/daemon.md` (the
desktop shell's updates), `README.md` (install the app), `CHANGELOG.md` (0.1.0, dated).

**Background commands.** `RunManager.command_ended` no longer calls `queue`; nothing of Dot's is ever stored in a chat's
queue. A run at work on the chat is told at its next step: `loop.py` takes the ended, untold commands of the chat
(`Terminals.take_ended`, once per session end) next to the peers note and stores a `[system note]` with the same words
the queued message had (`ended_notices`: which command, its exit status, how long it ran, nothing it printed); it is a
note from Dot, not the inbox, so it clears no taint and is no instruction. When no run of any process works on the chat,
nothing waits in its queue and the queue is not held, `RunManager._tell_ended_commands` starts the telling run directly
(source `background`, the chat's choices and agent, started as untrusted as the chat's last run ended) and tells the
pages with `queue_changed` and `started_run_id`, so the page follows it and nothing flashes in the Queued sheet;
`_follow_queue` calls it after `_drain` on a done end, for a command that ended in the run's last step. After a stop or
a failed run nothing is queued and nothing is held (the chat is no longer left "Paused until you resume it" with Dot's
row), and the next run of the chat, a queued message's or the owner's, is told at its first step; a start that another
start beat leaves the news to that run. The item 427 take-back of a queued notice is deleted with `command_read`,
`close_read` and `end_read`: a run that reads the end itself closes the session, which is never told. The owner's queued
messages and their order are untouched. The tool texts of `terminal_open` say: you are told at your next step, or in a
new run when none works on the chat. Tests: smoke (`test_background_commands.py`: idle case, working run told once at
its next step with nothing queued, end in the last step, stop then the owner's next run, close in the window, a beaten
start; `test_terminal.py`: an end is handed out once; `test_taint_goes_on.py`: the note clears no taint), the browser
test of the chat page unchanged, `dotx eval check`. Docs: `docs/runs.md`, `docs/safety.md`, `docs/daemon.md`,
`CHANGELOG.md` (Unreleased).

**The daemon log's bugs.** Item 437, part daemonlog, as built: nine recurring errors and warnings of the owner's own

Settings › Phone, asked for together, no longer crash: PyObjC binds a Core Graphics function the first time its name is
read and two worker threads reading it unbound at once made the second fail with a KeyError, so `qr.py` makes its

priced each call at the model's longest answer and refused it on an account with few credits, so the connector now asks
once more with the answer length the 402 names (at least 1,024 tokens) and logs `openrouter_max_tokens_lowered`. A
daemon that refuses its configuration says why where the owner looks: the error names each setting and says that a newer
Dot may add a key this version does not know, `dotx` writes a `command_failed` event to `dotx.log` for every command
that ends with an error (a failed daemon start included), `dotx service status` shows the failure that ended the latest
daemon when it does not answer, and `dotx service install` names it when the job loads but the daemon ended with an
error since the install began. The compaction check leaves a name the summary abbreviates (an ellipsis inside it, a

went away under the click says nothing, any other failure is `consent_decline_failed` with the page's address. Chrome's

warning. Left to a human because they sit in `review.py`: the retry note of a reviewer answer that was not usable still

### 441. `dotx service restart`: restart the daemon now, or once no run works

**Status: done (2026-10-20), on `item-441-restart-when-idle`, on the owner's word to find and fix the app's problems.**
Seen twice on the owner's Mac: a run that merged a change of Dot's own code wanted the daemon restarted once it had
ended, and improvised it with a shell script submitted as a launchd job (`launchctl submit -l
dev.dotagent.restart-after-run ... /tmp/dot-restart-after-run.sh`). `launchctl submit` keeps a job alive, so launchd
started the script again each time it exited and the daemon was restarted every 30 s while no run worked (312
`daemon_started` events in its log); the job was removed by hand. Dot had no command for "restart the daemon when no run
works". **As built.** `dotx service restart` restarts the installed daemon now: its job is unloaded (`bootout`: SIGTERM,
and launchctl waits until it has exited) and loaded again from its property list (`launchd.restart_job`), and the
command waits up to 60 s until a new process answers `/api/health`, then prints its version (a clear error naming `dotx
service install` when launchd has no job of it). `dotx service restart --when-idle` returns at once after it loads a
one-shot launchd job, `dev.dotagent.restart-when-idle`, from a property list in Dot's home (`RunAtLoad`,
`AbandonProcessGroup`, no `KeepAlive`, the running Python with `-P -m dotagent.restart_when_idle`, `DOT_HOME` and
`DOT_LOG_DIR` handed on when set). The program reads the database through a read-only SQLite connection every 5 s,
counting the runs in `WORKING_STATUSES` (the run that asked counts until it ends); once none works it restarts the
daemon as the command does, logs `restart_when_idle_waiting`, `_idle`, `_restarted`, `_gave_up` (after 2 hours, without
a restart), `_failed` or `_crashed` (an error that is not Dot's, with its traceback) to `dotx.log`, deletes its property
list and unloads its own label. A missing or unreadable database is an error, never an idle daemon. Asking while one is
on its way changes nothing, since replacing it could stop it between unloading the daemon's job and loading it again;
`dotx service status` has a `restart` line, and `dotx service uninstall` cancels a waiting one. The shell and terminal
tools mark the commands of a run (`DOT_RUN_SHELL`, `core/runenv.py`), and `dotx service restart` and `dotx service
install` refuse under it: the daemon would stop under the run and the run's end would kill the command between the
unload and the load (the pre-push review's finds, over two rounds). The shell tool's description tells the model to ask
for `--when-idle` and never to load a launchd job of its own, and where that cannot run (the sandbox outside yolo keeps
a run from launchctl) to say that the daemon needs `dotx service restart`. The hints that told `dotx service install` as
the way to restart (browser attach and detach, service permissions, the typed judge, Settings › Keys) say `dotx service
restart`. Tests: `tests/unit/test_restart_when_idle.py` (the plist, the idle check per status against a scratch store,
the wait, the program end to end, the restart as unload and load, a waiting restart left as it is, uninstall cancelling
it, the refusal in a run, the mark on a run's commands), against a stand-in `launchctl` and a local health check. Docs:
`docs/daemon.md` and the docs that told the restart.

### 443. In yolo nothing is asked: the agent does what it can itself

**Status: done (2026-10-20).** The owner's word of 2026-10-20, with two screenshots of a yolo run: Dot stopped to ask
them to type a one-time code it had already read from the mail, and a `browser_click` on "Send" waited for their yes
"in every mode, whatever your rules say". A yolo run is theirs to be done with: "eğer yapabileceği bir şey ise bana
sormasın, ayrıca izin de istemesin" — if it can do it, it does not ask, and it does not ask for permission.
**As built.** In the approval mode `yolo` nothing is asked (`agent/gate.py`): every layer below it — the always-on
review, Dot's own files, the guard of money and credentials and of a message or a post in the owner's name, a
pre-approved spend, a rule of the owner's that hands a step off — is waived, and the action's record keeps the reason it
would have asked for (`_waive`, one `approval_auto` row per step). A refusal is not a question and stands: a `research`
run's limit still refuses. (A rule of the owner's cannot refuse one — its behaviours are allow, preapproved, ask and
hand off — and the hand-off a rule asks for is waived with the rest.) The secret-field rule follows: the browser's batch, the
desktop's step and `terminal_send` type a password, a one-time code or a card's details themselves in a yolo run
(`desktop.actions.enter_secure_field`), where every other mode still refuses them and hands the field to the owner (item
429). The prompt says the same in the two lines a yolo run reads differently: the approvals line ("nothing waits for the
user … do what was asked yourself") and the rule of trust and safety about a field that takes a secret (a code it can
read or a password it was given, it types itself). `mode_gate`, the sandbox and everything else are as they were.
Tests: `tests/unit/test_guard.py`, `test_run_modes.py`, `test_rule_answers.py`, `test_supervised_and_own_files.py`,

### 451. A message sent on one screen shows at once on the other

**Status: done (2026-10-21).** The owner's word of 2026-10-21: a message sent on the phone did not show on the desktop
until the chat was left and opened again, and the same the other way round; fix that alone. **Cause.** A message sent to
a chat at rest starts the chat's next run (`POST /runs` with its thread); the screen it was sent from goes on at that
run, but a page of the same chat elsewhere follows only its own run's stream and was never told: the lifecycle stream's
`run_queued` carries no thread, and nothing read the chat again. A message queued while a run works already showed
everywhere (`queue_changed`), and a steer on the run's own stream. **As built** (`views/run.js`). A page that shows the
chat's newest run goes on at the newer one, as the screen it was sent from does: when a run of the chat is queued (it
reads the chat's newest runs once on a root `run_queued`), and once the lifecycle stream is back after a break, which
replays nothing (a phone put away). What was typed there and not sent goes with it as the newer run's draft (`moveDraft`
of `composer.js`). A page whose run was not the chat's newest when it first read the chat stays where it is: an earlier
run opened from the sidebar's Activity (a question it left, a lesson it drew), from a link or by its address, or a
delegated run; such a page reads the chat once. The tab keeps the run it showed as the chat's newest
(`dot.chatShown.<thread>` in its session storage) until the page leaves it, so a phone's page that the browser loads
again goes on from where it stood. Every way the page goes on (a message sent there, the queue's next one, an answer,
Continue, a rewind) takes one guard, so two of them at once open the run once. The pre-push review's first pass stopped
a page that took every page not reached by a link (main.js's history state) for the chat: the sidebar's Activity rows
count as no link, and a question left on an earlier run could no longer be answered there. Its second and third passes
found the same of questions: a page whose run left questions open stays for them, and once the last one closes, answered
there or on another screen or skipped, it looks again whether the chat went on (`paintQuestions`). Tests:
`tests/smoke/test_chat_follows.py` (Chrome wide and WebKit as a phone on one chat: the phone's message shows on the wide
window and the wide window's on the phone, the wide window's unsent words go with it, a page of the earlier run opened
by its address stays, and a phone's page loaded again after it showed the chat opens where the chat is; a run that left
two questions, open on both screens: the first answer keeps both pages there, the last, sent on the phone, opens the
chat's newest run on both; on main the wide window never moves). Docs: `docs/daemon.md`.

**Status: done (2026-10-21).** The owner's word of 2026-10-21: a message sent scrolls the chat up and down before it

### 449. The rules move with arrows, and a rule that never decides says so

**Status: done (2026-10-21).** The first of the nine ideas the owner took from the comparison with OpenBot
(`reports/openbot-vs-dot-2026-10-20.md`, local; the plan below), and the first step of its second, "the strictest rule
wins". The design, checked against the code and critiqued, does not make the strictest answer win: the order of the
rules is today the only way to write an exception (the Rules page's own examples, "let Dot run git status without
asking" above "ask me before rm", are an allow above a broader ask), and a stored rule carries no sign that an exception
was meant. It goes in three steps: the owner can move the rules and sees which of them never decide (this item); later,
once the owner has seen the notes for a release, a rule that hands the step over decides wherever it stands (on the
human path of `policy/`). **As built.** `Store.move_rule` moves a rule a number of places along the order, which it
reads under the write lock, and numbers the rules 1 to n, which closes the gaps deleted rules left; `POST
/api/rules/{id}/move` moves it one place up or down (422 past either end, 404 for no rule) and tells the pages
(`rules_changed`). `server/rule_shadow.py` names for each rule the earlier enabled rule that fits every action it fits
(no expression or the same one, on a tool pattern that takes in its own: `*`, the same pattern, or one that matches its
plain tool name), and `GET /api/rules` gives it as `never_decided_by`, computed once on the server and not again in the
page (the critique). Whether two different expressions overlap is not told. The policy is untouched: `match_rule` still
takes the first fit, and the rule the note names is the one that decides (the unit test reads it off `match_rule`). The
Rules page draws two arrows on a rule's row, off at the ends, that keep the focus as the rule moves (the other arrow
once it reaches an end), and a "Never decides" badge whose title names the rule that decides in its place. The note
above the rules said a yolo run keeps all of the protections that are always on but the first; since item 443 it keeps
only the second, a research run's limit, and the note says so. What a yolo run does is untouched. Tests:
`tests/unit/test_rule_shadow.py` (the certain cases, the cases not told, the note against the engine),
`tests/smoke/test_server.py` (a move, the numbering, the ends, 404, a direction that is none),
`tests/smoke/test_rules.py` (the page at 1280 and at 390 px, the phone a touch screen where a row's buttons always show,
in light and dark: the badge, the arrows, the focus). Docs: `docs/safety.md` (step 6), `docs/daemon.md`.

**The plan it starts.** The owner's go-ahead of 2026-10-20 and 21: the nine ideas, each in its own pull request, planned
so that today's Dot keeps working as it does, and yolo's freedom untouched ("YOLO modundaki serbestliğe dokunma"): in
yolo none of them adds a question, a refusal, a hand-off, a wait or a mask, a no given in another mode does not carry
into it, and each that touches the gate, the policy, the loop or what a run sees has a test that a yolo run does what it
did. The designs were written against the code by seven agents and critiqued; an item takes its number when it starts.
First, small and off the human paths: the money and credential floor of MCP tools (their names say a payment or a
credential), a no not asked again in the same run, the session cookies of Dot's own Chrome kept across its restarts
(cookies, sessions and history stay as in a real browser, for the Default profile and those the owner added, not
Incognito), a repeating schedule switched off after failed runs in a row, Run now with a schedule's past firings, and
this item. Then the medium ones: the values of password, one-time-code and card fields kept out of what the model reads
(not in yolo), every decision of the gate recorded on its step and a rule tried on past steps before it is added, a
notification level per schedule, an agent paused without losing it, a "while you were away" digest, scheduled work held
without the emergency stop, a schedule run as one of the owner's agents, and the owner driving Dot's browser from the
phone while the run is held. Last, the ones on the human paths, each waiting for the owner's yes: the release gated on
the whole gate with browser tests in CI and the workflows checked by zizmor, the rule that hands a step over deciding
wherever it stands, and approvals a run nobody watches keeps for the owner to answer later (off by default; never in
yolo, where nothing is asked; not for a message, a post, an MCP call or an upload, whose words a later yes would not
bind; and never by running the kept call outside its run).

### 453. Dot's own Chrome keeps its session cookies when it starts again

**Status: done (2026-10-21).** Part of the ninth of the nine ideas taken from OpenBot (item 449 has the plan), and the
owner's word of 2026-10-21, corrected after a first reading the wrong way round: "Hayır sen yanlış anladın silmesin" —
Dot's Chrome must keep cookies, sessions and history like a real browser, for Default and the profiles the owner added,
not for Incognito. Cookies with an expiry and the history already stayed; the cookies a site gives no expiry, where many
sites keep a sign-in, were gone after every restart of Dot's Chrome (the daemon's, the Mac's, an idle close). **Measured
first.** The design would have kept them in a file of its own (a 0600 copy of the jar, saved every 30 s and put back
before the first page), and the critique asked to try Chrome's own way before that: Chrome writes session cookies into
the profile while it runs and deletes them as it starts, unless its last run crashed, when it gives them back. On a
scratch profile (Chrome 155, Playwright 1.63, Dot's switches): a normal restart dropped the session cookie; with
`profile.exit_type` set to `Crashed` in the profile's preferences and `--hide-crash-restore-bubble` the cookie came
back, headless and with a window, after each of five restarts in a row, and no page of the last run was opened. **As
built.** `browser.profiles.keep_session_cookies` writes that word into the preferences of the profile (`exit_type`
`Crashed`, `exited_cleanly` false; the other preferences kept, written only when they say otherwise, and not for
Incognito nor a profile whose preferences hold nothing yet; a new profile whose zoom was just written gets it too, with
nothing to give back) before Dot's own Chrome starts (after the zoom, item 358) and before Sign in… and `dotx browser
login` open their window (`browser.login`), so a session cookie set in either survives the other; both start Chrome with
the switch. No copy of a cookie leaves Chrome's own store, which keeps them under the key it always used, so an imported
profile keeps them too. **Clear** still deletes them. Item 447 of another session (Dot's Chrome closed once unused)
ships with that close off; with this item in, the close loses no sign-in and its default can be 300 s, the owner's call.
Yolo and every approval mode are untouched. Tests: `tests/unit/test_browser_profiles.py` (the word written, the rest
kept, Incognito and a fresh profile left alone, a state Dot does not know refused),
`tests/smoke/test_browser_session_cookies.py` (a real Chrome on a throwaway profile: a cookie without an expiry is still
sent after Dot's Chrome starts again, and without the word it is not, while a dated one is in both). Docs:
`docs/browser-and-computer-use.md`.

schedule now, switched on or off, due or not, as a firing goes (unattended, the schedule's own choices, the digest of
its earlier runs), in a chat titled `<name> · <time> · by hand` (or the schedule's chat), its first message saying it

emergency stop is engaged and while a run of the schedule is at work or being started: a set of the schedules being
started, entered by a tick's firing and by a hand run alike, closes the window between the check and the run in flight,

are methods of their own, and `_firing_chat` takes its title. Routes: `POST /api/schedules/{id}/run` (201, a run), `GET
/api/schedules/{id}/firings` (its last runs, newest first, one at work among them, each with its chat's title,
`Store.schedule_firings`). On Schedules a row has a play button whose title says it does real work with the approvals
its run takes (yolo: "asking nothing"), with no question first, as the owner's word of 2026-10-21 asks of yolo ("YOLO
modundaki serbestliğe dokunma"): a click opens the run's page, where Stop is, and a toast says it started; **Firings**
opens the list under the row, kept open and read again as the list is painted again. The critique's corrections: the

page, the list). The scheduler's own tests pass unchanged. Docs: `docs/memory-and-schedules.md`, `docs/daemon.md`.

### 458. A repeating schedule whose runs keep failing is switched off, and you are told

**Status: done (2026-10-21).** The fifth of the nine ideas taken from OpenBot (item 449 has the plan), its second part:
"a repeating schedule switched off after N failed runs in a row". Today a schedule whose goal cannot be reached any more
(a site moved, a key expired) fails at every firing, unseen but for the end of each run. **As built.** A schedule keeps
how many of its runs in a row ended failed (`runs_failed_in_row`, a column; not derived from the last runs, so that
after the owner fixes the cause and switches it on again one more failure does not switch it straight off):
`Store.record_schedule_outcome` writes a run's end and the row together (`done` sets it to 0, `failed` adds one,
`cancelled` leaves it), in the watch of every run of the schedule, at its time and by hand alike (a run by hand that
ends done starts the row again, which is how the owner tries a fix). A firing that started no run counts not at all.
When a repeating schedule that is on reaches its limit (`ScheduleOptions.stop_after_failures`, its form's **Switch off
after**: 3, 5, 10, 20 or never; else `[scheduler] stop_after_failures`, 0 = never, which is how Dot worked), it is
switched off for good with the status "switched off: its last N runs failed" and the live event `schedule_stopped`, told
once by the phone and the desktop (the schedule is off afterwards); a one-time schedule is never switched off by it.
Switching a schedule on again, or changing it, starts its row afresh and clears that status. The row says "N failed in a
row", with when it switches itself off in its title; the form's default names the configured value
(`StatusView.schedule_stop_after_failures`). The critique's points taken: the counter moves for every schedule and only
the switch-off is the repeating ones'; the event is sent only when the switch-off changed the row; the column is named
apart from the failures to start of `scheduler/failures.py`. Not done: the critique's one tuple of option columns, left
for the notification level, which adds the next option. Yolo is untouched: a yolo schedule's runs count as any other's,
and nothing is asked. Tests: `tests/unit/test_schedule_stop.py` (the limit, the rule, the store's row),
`tests/unit/test_push.py` (the phone's message), `tests/smoke/test_schedule_stop.py` (through the routes and a real
scheduler: two failed and one done, a timed firing's failure counting, the third in a row switching off a yolo schedule
with one event, switching it on again; a one-time schedule and one without a limit kept on; the page at 1280 px and at
390 px as a touch screen: the row's note and the form's limit). Docs: `docs/memory-and-schedules.md`, `docs/daemon.md`,
`defaults.toml`.
